analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and insurers to publish negotiated prices and give patients a free cost-estimator tool.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee markup or a Senate vote; it sat with the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee from April 2021 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law requirements that hospitals publish a full list of standard charges — including the rates they negotiated with each insurer, the discounted cash price, and billing codes — for at least 300 services that patients can schedule in advance. It would also require health insurance plans to publish in-network and out-of-network rates, the net prices they pay for prescription drugs after rebates, and to offer a free online tool that tells a patient what a service will cost them before they get it. Hospitals that do not comply would face a civil fine of up to $300 per day.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients shopping for scheduled care, people paying cash without insurance, and employers buying coverage. Today a hospital's listed 'sticker' price often bears little relation to what insurers actually pay, and patients usually cannot learn their out-of-pocket cost until the bill arrives. The bill would force that information into the open so people can compare prices before choosing a provider.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals must publish, in a free machine-readable format, the gross charge, each insurer's negotiated rate, the discounted cash price, and billing codes for at least 300 shoppable services, or maintain an online price-estimator tool that does the same [S3].
Insurance plans must disclose in-network rates, out-of-network allowed amounts, and the net prices paid for prescription drugs after rebates and discounts are allocated [S2] [S3].

Plans must provide a free real-time online tool that tells an individual their estimated cost-sharing for a covered item or service from a specific provider, and must answer paper requests by mail within two business days [S3].
Hospitals that fail to comply after a corrective action plan would face a civil monetary penalty of up to $300 per day of ongoing violation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and health insurers. Hospitals would bear the cost of publishing hundreds of negotiated rates and could no longer rely on price opacity when negotiating with insurers and patients. Insurers would have to disclose what they actually pay providers and drugmakers, which weakens their bargaining position and exposes their drug-rebate economics.

drawbacks.text: The maximum fine for a hospital that ignores the requirement is only $300 per day, a cap that is small relative to a hospital's budget, so enforcement could be weak [S3].

Hospitals would face real compliance costs in publishing and maintaining price files for at least 300 shoppable services and an estimator tool, and disclosing every insurer's negotiated rate can undercut a hospital's ability to negotiate discounts privately [S3].

The bill itself requires notices telling patients that an estimate is not a guarantee of benefits and that actual charges may differ from the estimate, an honest acknowledgment that transparency helps comparison shopping but does not fix billing surprises [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — letting patients and employers see real prices before care — is modest but real, and the costs fall mostly on industries that profit from price secrecy. The main design weakness is enforcement: a $300-per-day cap is unlikely to change a large hospital system's behavior, so the bill relies more on public shaming than on penalties. It also largely codifies transparency rules the executive branch already adopted, so its practical value is making them permanent statute rather than creating something new.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2021 and referred to the Senate health committee, which never took it up, so it died without a markup or a vote when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Braun introduced the bill on April 29, 2021, joined by four Republican cosponsors: Senators Grassley, Ernst, Barrasso, and Tillis [S1] [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where it received no further action [S5].
No committee markup, floor vote, or House action ever occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and health insurers are better off, because their negotiated rates never had to be published under a permanent statute; patients still only have transparency rules that future administrations could weaken, and the committee that never acted faced no vote on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals and insurers keep price secrecy

for.name: Mike Braun
for.role: U.S. Senator from Indiana; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

against.name: Patty Murray
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill died without action in the Democratic-chaired health committee.

industries.note: The bill would require hospitals to publish every insurer's negotiated rate, their discounted cash price, and charges for at least 300 shoppable services, with fines for noncompliance. Hospitals' interest lies in keeping those rates confidential so they can charge different payers different amounts; the public's interest is seeing the prices before care.

The bill would force insurers to disclose in-network and out-of-network rates and the net prices they pay for prescription drugs, and to give members a free real-time cost estimator. Insurers gain bargaining leverage from keeping those numbers private, which is exactly what the bill takes away.

The bill's definition of negotiated rates includes rates set through pharmacy benefit managers, and requires disclosure of the net price a plan pays for a drug after rebates and fees. That would expose spread pricing and rebate economics that currently stay hidden from patients.
